system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 4 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2178-07-13 16:04:00 to 2178-07-17 12:40:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted with Enterobacter bacteremia, likely originating from his tunneled central venous catheter, which was confirmed by positive tip culture. He also had multifocal pneumonia and worsening ascites requiring multiple therapeutic paracenteses. He developed acute kidney injury, consistent with hepatorenal syndrome type 2, which stabilized with albumin and discontinuation of diuretics. His portopulmonary hypertension worsened, with echocardiogram showing increased pulmonary artery pressure. He completed a 14-day course of IV antibiotics, with clearance of bacteremia. His condition improved, and he was discharged home on oral ciprofloxacin for SBP prophylaxis, with plans for outpatient follow-up, repeat blood cultures, and eventual tunneled line replacement.
problems: Bloodstream infection due to central venous catheter
Other septicemia due to gram-negative organisms
Cirrhosis of liver without mention of alcohol

radiology_notes.text:
CHEST RADIOGRAPH

INDICATION:  PICC line placement.

COMPARISON:  ___.

FINDINGS:  Compared to the previous radiograph, the previous PICC line on the
right has been removed and replaced by a new PICC line.  The tip of the PICC
line projects over the mid SVC.  The previously placed left central venous
catheter has been removed.  The lung volumes remain low.  There are areas of
atelectasis at both lung bases.  No evidence of pneumonia or pulmonary edema. 
Unchanged size of the cardiac silhouette.  There is no evidence of
pneumothorax or other complications.

INDICATION:  ___ man with end-stage liver disease, hepatopulmonary
syndrome and portopulmonary hypertension, on Remodulin; please place tunneled
CVL for Remodulin, please place single lumen with volume measurements.  In
addition, please perform paracentesis and remove 5 liters.

PHYSICIANS:  Dr.  ___ (radiology fellow) and Dr. ___
___ (radiology attending) who was present throughout and supervised
the procedure.

MEDICATION:  The procedure was performed under moderate conscious sedation,
the patient received 125 mcg of fentanyl and 2.5 mg of Versed for the total
intraservice time of 30 minutes, during which time the patient's hemodynamic
parameters were continuously monitored.

RADIATION:  11 mGy, 1 minute 53 seconds of fluoroscopy time.

PROCEDURES:
1.  Therapeutic paracentesis, 5 liters removed.
2.  Placement of a triple-lumen tunneled access line.

PROCEDURE DETAILS:
Following discussion of the risks, benefits, and alternatives to the
procedure, informed written patient consent was obtained.  The patient was
brought to the angiographic suite and placed supine on the table.  A
pre-procedure timeout was performed using three patient identifiers.  The skin
of the right abdomen and right neck was prepped and draped in the usual
sterile fashion.  Initially, we performed the paracentesis.

Ultrasound was used to select an appropriate target.  Approximately 1 cc of 1%
lidocaine was infiltrated into the skin and subcutaneous tissues for local
anesthesia.  Using direct ultrasound visualization, a 5 ___ ___ catheter
was advanced into the peritoneal cavity.  20 cc of ascitic fluid were
withdrawn for the requested lab tests.  The catheter was attached to suction
and 5 liters of fluid were removed.  Following this, the ___ catheter was
removed and a sterile dressing was applied.  There were no immediate
post-procedure complications.

We then proceeded to place the tunneled central line.  Approximately 2 cc of
1% lidocaine were infiltrated into the skin and subcutaneous tissues overlying
the right internal jugular vein.  A micropuncture needle was placed in the
right internal jugular vein and a nitinol wire was advanced readily through
the needle.  A small skin incision was made and the needle was exchanged for a
micropuncture sheath.  The inner portion of the sheath was removed along with
the wire and ___ wire was advanced through the sheath through the central
veins into the IVC.  A further 2 cc of 1% lidocaine was infiltrated into the
skin and subcutaneous tissues over the right anterior chest wall.  A small
skin incision was made, approximately 6 cc of 1% lidocaine with epinephrine
was infiltrated along the planned tunneling route.  A single-lumen catheter
was selected and cut to an appropriate length.  The flush volume was measured
as 1.1 mL.  The catheter tubing was attached to a tunneling device and passed
in the right anterior chest wall incision to the neck.  Dilatation over the
___ wire was performed after removal of the micropuncture sheath using an 8
___ dilator followed by placement of a 10 ___ peel-away sheath.  The
inner portion of the sheath was removed along with the wire as the catheter
tubing was advanced centrally.  The peel-away sheath was gradually removed. 
The catheter tubing was advanced.  Following completion of this maneuver, the
tip was in the right atrium.  The catheter was secured to the skin with 0 silk
suture and a Flexi-Trak.  The venotomy site was closed using subcuticular ___
Vicryl.  Sterile dressings were applied to both sites.  Both lumens were
aspirated and flushed without difficulty.  There were no immediate
post-procedure complications.

IMPRESSION:
1.  Diagnostic and therapeutic paracentesis with removal of 5 liters of clear
yellow ascitic fluid.
2.  Technically successful placement of a single-lumen tunneled access line. 
The catheter volume is 1.1 mL.

TYPE OF EXAMINATION:  Chest, AP portable single view.

INDICATION:  ___ male patient with recent Dobbhoff line placement,
check position.

FINDINGS:  AP single view of the chest has been obtained with patient in
semi-upright position.  Analysis is performed in direct comparison with the
next preceding similar study of ___.  During the latest interval, a
Dobbhoff line has been placed, seen to pass well below the diaphragm.  The
Dobbhoff line follows the curve of the stomach and apparently has passed the
pylorus as its distal portion assumes the contours of the duodenal loop.  The
line escapes in the lower limit of the image and cannot be followed.  It does
not appear in the area of the proximal jejunal loops.

Pulmonary appearance is unchanged.  Right-sided PICC line as before.  Other
lines are apparently external overlying the chest.

IMPRESSION:  Dobbhoff line reaching beyond pylorus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___. I'm Dr. ___, one of your hospital doctors. I see you're here because of poor nutrition and to get a feeding tube and a new line for your treprostinil.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I’ve been losing weight and just can’t eat much. Food tastes bad since I started the treprostinil.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. That’s a known side effect. We’re going to help you with a Dobhoff tube so you can get nutrition even if you’re not eating well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my tunneled line? I’ve been using the PICC, but it’s not ideal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll replace the tunneled line tomorrow. It’s safer for long-term treprostinil use. The PICC is temporary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I manage the pump myself, so I want it to be reliable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You do a great job managing it. We’ll make sure the new line is secure and ready for home use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs show low white blood cells and platelets, which is expected with cirrhosis. We’ll monitor that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had low platelets for a while. Is it safe to do the procedures?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll use normal platelets if needed. The team is aware, and we’ll take precautions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also noticed your kidney function has improved. Creatinine is now 1.2, much better than before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I was worried after last time with the kidney issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, last admission was tough with the infection and pneumonia. But you cleared the bacteremia, and now we’re focusing on getting you stronger for transplant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I really want to be ready. That’s why I want the feeding tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Nutrition is key. The team recommends Isosource at 65 cc/hr once the tube is placed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We just finished the paracentesis and tunneled line placement. Five liters of fluid were removed, and the new line is in place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How did it go? I was asleep, but I feel okay now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It went very well. The line is single-lumen, volume 1.1 mL, and it’s already connected. Treprostinil is running through it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. And the fluid removal? My belly felt so full.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the ascites was significant. The fluid looked clean, and the white count was low—no sign of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no spontaneous bacterial peritonitis this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, the culture came back negative. You’re on ciprofloxacin for prevention, which is helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep monitoring your oxygen too. You’re still on nighttime O2 for hepatopulmonary syndrome.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I use it every night. My pulse ox was 93 on room air yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s why we keep the O2. It helps with the low oxygen levels from liver disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. We placed the Dobhoff tube yesterday during endoscopy. The X-ray confirms it’s past the pylorus, in good position.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t feel a thing. Is it safe to start the feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve started Isosource at 65 cc/hr. We’ll keep an eye on your stomach for any bloating or discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll keep taking megace? It’s helped my appetite a little.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll continue megace, mirtazapine, and fluoxetine. They help with appetite and mood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your liver numbers are stable. MELD is around 13, which is good for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Lower than last time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, last admission it was 17. Your kidney function improved, which helps lower the score.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s good for transplant listing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It means your body is more stable. We want you strong and well-nourished when a liver becomes available.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs today look better. Creatinine is down to 0.9, and bicarbonate is normalizing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Any change in the feeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, we’re keeping the feeds at goal. You’re tolerating them well—no vomiting or diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your platelets are up to 30, still low but stable. No need for transfusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my back pain? It’s been okay with the morphine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll keep your MS Contin and dilaudid for breakthrough. Osteoporosis and old fractures make it chronic, but we can manage it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also checked your calcium and vitamin D. You’re on supplements, which is important.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I take them every day. Don’t want more fractures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—discharge today. You’re doing well. The feeding tube and new line are working, and you’ve had no complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your meds, including ciprofloxacin, lactulose, and rifaximin. The feeding will continue at 65 cc/hr.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The supply company will deliver your tube feeds and pump supplies today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the tunneled line care?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep the dressing clean and dry. Change it weekly or if wet. Call if redness, swelling, or fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Weigh yourself daily. Call if you gain more than 3 pounds in a day—could be fluid building up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, labs in a few days—chem 10, CBC, coags, liver tests. Fax them to your hepatology team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure my sister helps me with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: She’s listed as your contact—good to have support. Keep all your transplant clinic appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m hopeful. I feel better already with the feeds starting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the goal. Nutrition, stability, and readiness. You’re on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll see you in follow-up. Take care, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. The discharge nurse will go over everything one more time before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, sounds good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—keep using sildenafil and the oxygen at night. They help your lung pressures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I haven’t missed a dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. That’s all for now. Rest up and keep building your strength.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye, Doctor.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted for placement of a Dobhoff feeding tube and replacement of his tunneled central line due to malnutrition and ongoing treprostinil therapy for portopulmonary hypertension. He reported significant anorexia and weight loss attributed to treprostinil, despite using megestrol to improve appetite. A tunneled line was successfully placed on hospital day two, and a Dobhoff tube was inserted endoscopically the following day, with radiographic confirmation of correct placement. Tube feeds were initiated and tolerated well. Five liters of ascitic fluid were removed during paracentesis, with no signs of infection. His kidney function improved, with creatinine normalizing, and liver enzymes remained stable. He was discharged home with services to continue tube feeds, treprostinil via the new line, and all home medications, including ciprofloxacin for SBP prophylaxis. Outpatient follow-up and lab monitoring were arranged.
